Page oneHome — the autumn the garden began

Fall first, then the year turns. Down by the gate of Wee's cottage is one square of dug earth, waiting — and this is the story of what grew in it.

🌱 Begin the season

Fifteen pages, one garden, no way to spoil any of it. Pipkin — the little round creature, all grown now — will walk beside you, the way he did in the first book.

✦ This telling is a grown-Pipkin try-out: he guides on page four, remembers on page six, and reaches on page ten.

Page twoThe Market — seeds in paper packets

This little piggie went to market… for seeds. Margo's stall stands at the harbour market: paper packets on strings, a brass scale, and a jar of bulbs like onions in coats.

Early autumn, apples dropping, first cool wind off the sea. Choose your packets, count your seeds, and mind the buttons in Wee's pocket — Margo trades kindly.

🧺 Margo's stall

The sunflower packet is already Wee's own — one of her three. Tap two more packets to keep.

Now count the sunflower seeds into the packet — tap each one:

Counted: 0 of 5

✔ Three packets chosen, five seeds counted. The bed at home is dug already — garlic and tulip bulbs are tucked under straw, asleep till spring.

Page threeThe Square — planting Wee's own

Home to plant. One square by the gate is Wee's own, and the sunflower is hers to name — every seed deserves a name, and this one will grow between the pages, all season long.

The plant only ever moves forward. Watering is affection, not upkeep — growth is tied to turning the page, and if you are ever busy, the rain looks after it.

Wee's Own Square
bare dug earth, full of promise

🌻 Planting

First, a name:

✔ Tucked in and watered. She will grow a little at every page you turn — watch for her.

Page fourFirst Water — the rhythm of the can

This little piggie stayed home… and listened to the garden drink. Watering a new seed is a small music: pour, and plink, and pour again.

The can has a song — three notes, and it only sings when a pour is true. Watch the ring: it swells like a held breath, and when it glows inside the golden band, that is the moment to tip the can. Pour outside the band and it is a splash for the stones — they were thirsty too. Nothing here can be done wrong; some pours sing, and some pours splash.

Wee's Own Square
the puddle grows with every true pour

🪣 The swelling ring — pour true

The ring swells like a held breath. Tip the can while it glows inside the golden band and the pour is true — one note of the can's song. Three true pours fill the song. Outside the band? A splash for the stones — they were thirsty too.

♪♪♪
0 / 3 true

✔ Three true pours — the can's whole song, sung into the soil. Under the ground, something small has decided to begin.

Page fiveSprout — a gentle search

While you were away, the page turned — and pages are how gardens grow here. Somewhere in the square, under one of these tufts, two small leaves are bowing hello.

Lift the tufts one by one. Stones are only napping; the sprout is shy, not lost. Nothing in this garden is ever lost — it is just late.

Wee's Own Square
the tufts keep the square's secrets

🔎 Find the sprout

Tap a tuft to peek beneath it.

✔ Found — two leaves, bowing hello. "Look," says Pipkin. "She remembers being watered."

Page sixWee Weeds — weed, or keep?

Spring, and everything is growing at once — including the things nobody planted. Wee kneels in the square with her trug, and Pipkin, who knows every leaf by sight, advises.

Sort each newcomer: into the square if it is a friend, or down by the fence if it is a weed. Weeds are not villains — the fence corner gets rain too. There is no way to sort wrongly for long; Pipkin will always tell you true.

Wee's Own Square
the sunflower minds none of it, and grows

🧺 From the Market — already here, in the square

Settled 0 / 0 🌼 🌼

🧤 The sorting

Sorted 0 / 6

✔ Six sorted, nobody scolded. The fence corner is blooming in its own way, and the square is all the sunflower's.

Page sevenThe Dry Week — carrying water

Then came the dry week, when the sun sat on the garden like a warm cat and would not move. The well is not far — just across the brook, over the stepping stones. The bucket is not heavy. It is only a matter of one brave journey.

While you were away she grew leaves — look at her. Now, the journey: cross the brook stone by stone — hop, tiptoe, or splash across, as you please — fill the bucket at the well, and carry it home to pour. One journey, there and back. And unfold the big leaf, for shade, the way Hazel shades her sill.

Wee's Own Square — the dry week
🍃
the soil is pale, and patient

🪨 The stepping-stone journey

Five stones cross the brook to the well. At every stone, choose how to land — hop, tiptoe, or splash. There is no wrong way over; there is only your way.

🌱 the squarethe well ⛲

Journey: stone 0 / 5 · no shade yet

✔ One journey — five stones, a full bucket carried home, and shade besides. As the water sinks in, the first cloud of the week stands up on the horizon to watch.

Page eightRain — the garden drinks itself

And then, in the night, the rain came back — the kind that looks after things while everyone is busy sleeping.

A quiet page. Watch the rain, and tap the puddles to make ripples. The rain looked after it while you were busy — it always does, in this garden.

tap the wet earth — ripples answer

🌧 Ripples

✔ Seven ripples, and the whole square shining. Somewhere under the wet leaves, the sunflower is drinking in her sleep.

Page nineBees — high summer's errands

High summer, bees, long evenings, warm stones. The garden is full of small errands, and the bee has five of them, written nowhere, remembered exactly.

Tap a flower and the bee will visit it. Any order pleases her — bees keep their own lists, and every flower gets its turn.

🐝

🌸 Five flowers

Visited: 0 / 5

✔ Five visits, five thank-yous. This is how sunflowers get seeds, by the way — the bee is carrying next year around in her pockets.

Page tenTall — the ribbon unrolls

While you were away, she did the quiet part: she became a bud on a tall green tower, holding her breath, kindly.

Every garden needs measuring, and every measuring needs a ribbon and someone to say the sizes out loud. Unroll it four times, the way Pipkin does.

Page elevenBloom — the sunflower opens

One more kind tending, Pipkin said, back when she was a seed. This is the page it was about.

Tap the bud, gently, three times. Flowers open the way good news arrives — a little at a time, then all at once. Watch Pipkin, too.

Wee's Own Square
tap the bud — three gentle taps

🌻 Opening

Taps: 0 / 3

The bud is listening.

✔ Oh — oh, look at that. You grew that. We grew that. And did you see? The little pink bud on Pipkin's own sprout has opened too.

🌱 Pipkin kept the rhythm while you were away — one of the three taps is his.

Page twelveBirds — share, or shoo kindly

A flower full of seeds is a rumour, and birds always hear rumours first. Three of them land on the fence, polite as anything, and wait to see what kind of garden this is.

Both choices are kind ones, and the garden has enough for either. Share a few seeds now — or wave Pipkin's ribbon, gently, and let the birds sing from the tree instead. Choose as you like; you cannot choose wrong.

🐦 The fence, at teatime

✔ The garden keeps both its seeds and its songs. That is the whole trick of gardens, and of most things.

Page thirteenHarvest — seeds into the tin

Late summer turning to autumn, seedheads papery, light gone gold. The flower bows — not tired, generous — and offers her seeds to whoever shakes gently.

Tap the flower head and shake: one seed, two seeds, sometimes three, each landing in the tin with a small bright tink. Twelve seeds fill the tin — next year, and a friend's, kept safe.

Wee's Own Square
tap the flower — shake, and tink

🥫 The seed tin

Seeds in the tin: 0 / 12

The tin is empty, and hopeful.

✔ Twelve seeds, kept. The tin has a name painted on it, and the name is the flower's own.

Page fourteenSharing — six places at the table

This little piggie had none — so everyone shared. That was the fourth piggie's page in the first book, and it is the garden's turn now: the harvest goes round the table, plate by plate.

Tap a plate to give it seeds from the tin — two each, fair and round. Five piggies… and count the plates again. There is a sixth place, small, at the far end, with a blue napkin. It was room, left on purpose. It gets seeds too.

🍽 Two seeds each

Seeds left in the tin: 12

✔ Every plate full — including the sixth, which was never an accident. Nobody at this table has none. Not anymore.

Page fifteenHome by the Brook — the season's rhyme

And this little piggie cried "wee, wee, wee!" all the way home — by the brook, as the light failed, with a tin of seeds for next year knocking softly in her pocket.

The year has turned: the opening painting, a year later, the bed full and gone to seed. Tap the fireflies, keep the rhyme, and come back whenever — the garden remembers its friends.

The season's rhyme — a keepsake
This little piggie went to market, for seeds in paper packets bright; this little piggie stayed home, and kept them warm all night; this little piggie planted hers, in her own square by the gate; this little piggie had none — so the others shared, and filled her plate; and this little piggie cried "wee, wee, wee!" all the way home by the brook, with seeds for next year.
